Module 2: Making Decisions (Conditionals)

2.1 Python Booleans:
Introduction to Booleans
Welcome to Module 2! 🧠
In Module 1, your programs followed a straight line from top to bottom, running every single command in order. But in real life, computers have to make choices all the time:
Is the player’s health zero? If yes, show "Game Over!"
Did the user type the correct password? If yes, unlock the phone.
Is the room temperature above 30°C? If yes, turn on the air conditioner.
To make smart decisions, computers need a way to answer simple Yes or No questions. In programming, we do this using a special data type called Booleans.
Click Next Lesson to discover how Booleans work!
Understanding Booleans
A Boolean (named after the mathematician George Boole) is the simplest data type in Python. Unlike numbers that can be infinite, a Boolean can hold only one of two possible values:
True (represents YES / ON)
False (represents NO / OFF)
Output
Two Golden Rules for Booleans:
Always Capitalize the First Letter: You must write True and False with a capital T and F. Writing true or false in lowercase will cause a NameError.
Booleans Are Not Strings: Never wrap them in quotes!
True is a real Boolean.
"True" is just plain text (a string).
Booleans Are Reserved Keywords: You cannot use True or False as variable names (e.g., True = 50 will throw a SyntaxError).

Boolean Expressions
How do we actually get True or False in real code? We ask Python questions using Boolean Expressions!
A Boolean expression is any piece of code that Python evaluates and answers with either True or False.
Think of it like asking a referee:
"Is 10 greater than 5?"  The referee says: True
"Is 3 equal to 8?"  The referee says: False
Click Next Lesson to see how we compare values and variables to create these expressions!

2.2 Comparison Operators

Introduction

Have you ever compared two things to make a decision?

Is my score higher than the high score?

Is the temperature cold enough for a jacket?

Did I enter the exact secret passkey?

In Python, we compare two quantities using Comparison Operators.

A comparison operator takes two values, compares them, and reports back a simple verdict: True or False.

Click Next Lesson to see the complete toolkit of comparison operators!

List of Comparison Operators

Python gives you six standard comparison tools:

Let's master them step by step!

Comparison Operators: > and >=

> (Strictly Greater Than): Returns True only if the left number is strictly bigger than the right number.

>= (Greater Than or Equal To): Returns True if the left number is bigger OR exactly equal to the right number.

Output

Notice that speed > 60 is False, but speed >= 60 is True because the = part allows a tie!

Comparison Operators: < and <=

< (Strictly Less Than): Returns True only if the left value is smaller than the right value.

<= (Less Than or Equal To): Returns True if the left value is smaller OR equal to the right value.

Comparison Operators: ==

To check if two values are equal, Python uses double equals ==.

Output

Crucial Warning:

= (Single Equals): Used for assignment (putting a value inside a variable).

== (Double Equals): Used for comparison (asking: "Are these two equal?").

Comparison Operators: !=

The != operator means Not Equal To. Think of the exclamation mark ! as meaning "NOT".

It returns:

True if the two values are different.

False if the two values are identical.

Output

  is True. Because they are identical,  is False. |

Using == and != With Strings

You can also compare text strings with == and !=. But keep in mind:

Capitalization Matters (Case-Sensitive):

"Falcon" == "Falcon"  True

"Falcon" == "falcon"  False (capital F is different from small f!)

Data Types Matter:

"10" == 10  False (a text string is never equal to a number!)

| D: "Cyber" |

2.3 Logical Operators

Introduction

In the previous lesson, we checked one condition at a time (like score > 80).

But real-world decisions usually require checking more than one thing at the same time:

To ride the mega roller-coaster, you must be taller than 130 cm AND wearing a safety belt.

To get into a weekend coding workshop, you need a student pass OR a guest invitation.

To launch a drone outdoors, it must NOT be raining.

When you need to combine two or more conditions together, Python uses Logical Operators.

Click Next Lesson to meet the three logical operators!

List of Logical Operators

Python gives you three simple, English-like words to combine conditions:

Let’s explore each operator one by one!

Logical Operator: and

The and operator is strict. Both conditions on either side must evaluate to True. If even one condition is False, the entire result becomes False!

Plaintext

True  and True   ---> True  (Both agree!)

True  and False  ---> False (One failed!)

False and True   ---> False (One failed!)

False and False  ---> False (Both failed!)

Output

2.4 if-else and elif Statements

The if Statement

Until now, your programs printed True or False. But a real app doesn't just print a verdict—it takes action!

An if statement allows your program to make a decision:

If the condition is True, Python runs the special code block inside it.

If the condition is False, Python completely skips that code and moves on!

Basic Syntax:

Notice the Two Magic Details:

The Colon (:): Every if line must end with a colon.

Indentation (4 spaces): The code belonging to the if block must be pushed inward with spaces (indented). That’s how Python knows what code belongs inside the decision!

Common Errors in Decision Making

Watch out for these 3 common bugs when writing conditions:

1. Forgetting the Colon (:):

Fix: Always put a colon : at the end of if, elif, and else lines.

2. Confusing = and ==:

Fix: Use == (double equals) to check equality!

3. Mismatched Indentation:

Fix: Always indent statements inside the block by 4 spaces.

Revision: The Decision-Making Cheat Sheet

Here is your master recap for controlling program flow:

if: Checks a condition. Runs its block only if the condition is True.

else: Runs when the if condition is False.

elif: Adds extra conditions to check in order. Only the first True branch runs.

Indentation (4 spaces): Tells Python which statements belong inside which branch.

Colons (:): Must be placed at the end of every if, elif, and else statement.

Variable Safety: Always initialize variables before an if block, or ensure they are assigned in an else branch to avoid NameError!
